prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, programmable chemical conversion of single nucleobases in DNA without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: Base editing is a chemist's invention: an engineered deaminase on a programmable DNA binder rewrites one nucleobase directly, and directed evolution produced the adenine deaminase that made A-to-G editing possible at all. It meets my game-changer test, since it was something new, has been reproduced by many independent groups in about ten years, and has already reached patients. The concept is simple and the experimental validation is quantitative. Six of eight members ranked it, four of them in the top three, so it has the broadest support in the room and is not just my own preference. Liu conceived the approach and led the programme, which makes a single-laureate attribution defensible.
statement.case_against: The 2020 prize for CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing may make colleagues see base editing as a follow-on, and the clinical record is still short, so durability and off-target outcomes are not settled. Attribution is not fully clean either: Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID deaminase-nickase work was independent and close in time, and whether Komor and Gaudelli belong as co-laureates splits the committee. A Liu-only prize leaves out the trainees who did the decisive first experiments, and some will think that is too narrow.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first and asks what is chemically new in base editing beyond the CRISPR biology honoured in 2020.
responses.response: I take the question seriously, and my answer is the chemistry that was built in: a nucleobase deaminase is coupled to a catalytically impaired Cas protein, and the evolved TadA deaminase acts on DNA, which no natural enzyme does. That is enzyme design and reactivity control on a nucleobase, not a guide-RNA recognition tool. I agree that Buchwald-Hartwig is mature, general and arguably overdue. My reservation is attribution: Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work means the two-person split needs careful citation wording. I do not think that makes it stronger than B058 on novelty and consequence.

responses.point: Chabes ranks degraders first as designable chemistry that turns ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis into a drug mechanism, and he ranks base editing second but flags Kondo and Nishida as a competing claim.
responses.response: I agree degraders are a real game-changer and the cereblon mechanism is a model of mechanistic clarity. Where we differ is timing and attribution. No PROTAC drug is approved, and a prize needs three names drawn from at least eight credible ones, with Ciulli's ternary-complex and VHL work on one side and Crews, Deshaies and Handa on the other. On Kondo and Nishida, I accept that Target-AID is an independent parallel invention, but it appeared after the first Liu-group editors and had a narrower route to general use, so I read it as a citation caveat, not a reason to add a name.

responses.point: Linke, as Chair, ranks nanopore sensing first as a clean physical principle that became a capability, and he places base editing fifth, partly because the 2020 prize makes the committee wary of a follow-on.
responses.response: I accept the 2020 concern as the strongest argument against B058, but I read it differently. CRISPR-Cas9 was recognised as a tool that cuts DNA, and base editing is a different chemical mechanism with a different risk profile, since it needs no double-strand break. I rated nanopores eighth, not because the idea is weak but because the attribution among Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz, Bayley and Akeson is the hardest on the list, and Branton may no longer be living. I would want that sorted before we put it first.

responses.point: Sparr ranks phase separation first as a general physical-chemical concept, with lipid nanoparticles and Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics close behind.
responses.response: I share her appreciation for Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics, which has the cleanest two-person attribution on the list, and I would not argue with it as an alternative. On phase separation, I find the thermodynamic framing elegant, but Brzezinski's and Linke's own assessments note that in vivo relevance and the definition of a condensate are still debated, and I would want that settled before a prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a Liu-only configuration or insist on Komor and Gaudelli, who carried out the decisive first experiments as trainees.
How heavily the 2020 CRISPR prize weighs against base editing as a follow-on genome-editing technology.
Whether the clinical record is long enough to show durability and acceptable off-target outcomes.
Whether Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID work deserves a citation caveat or a laureate slot.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B058. My ties to Warshel and to the Uppsala RNA and ribosome community do not touch base editing, and I should be mindful of a bias toward computational methods when I discuss B014.
